title: What a same-day response should mean
excerpt: A same-day response is a human email that names the next step, sent the day you write. The design itself stays on the project schedule.
alt: A person in a purple shirt typing on a bright blue laptop at a round table, writing a reply while the question is still the same day.
caption: Same day means a person answers with the next step, while the question is still fresh. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a same-day response include?
faqs.answer: A human acknowledgment of the actual question, a one- or two-sentence reading of the work, and a next step the sender can act on. If a price or a date would be a guess, the reply says what information would make the answer real. A template that could answer any founder still leaves the sender waiting.

faqs.question: Does same-day mean the design will be finished that day?
faqs.answer: A same-day response is a reply with the next step, from a person who has read the note. A homepage, a logo, or a technical plan is the project, and it belongs on a scoped date. Hanabi's same-day promise is that email reply.

faqs.question: What should a founder send so the reply is useful?
faqs.answer: Who the site or product is for, the one action it should earn, the current URL if one exists, and the timing you are actually facing. Three sentences are enough. A long deck asks for unpaid synthesis before anyone can answer.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Design studio communication includes a same-day response: a human answer, sent the same day, that names the next step. Hanabi offers that response by email. The promise is about being met by a person who has read what you sent. A finished design by dinner is a different promise, and it belongs to a scoped project with its own date.

The word "responsive" gets misunderstood when it is treated as a synonym for instant production. Speed of reply and speed of craft solve different problems. Founders need both, at different moments, described in plain words.

## What the reply contains

A useful same-day reply has four parts, and it can still be short.

It acknowledges the actual question. A template that could answer any founder is a slower form of silence, because the reader has to ask again.

It states what the studio understands the work to be. One or two sentences. A marketing site, a store migration, a product interface, a brand system. If the note was ambiguous, the reply says what was assumed.

It names the next step. That might be a time for an intro call, a request for the current URL, or a clear no because the work is a poor fit. A next step is a decision the sender can act on today.

It names what the reply is withholding. If a price, a date, or a sitemap would be a guess, the reply says the guess is premature and what information would make it real. Honesty about the missing piece is the response. An invented number would be faster and worse.

## What same-day work is allowed to exclude

The reply does not include a homepage, a logo, or a technical plan. Those are the project. Producing them inside a day, before fit is known, is how studios train founders to expect free strategy and then resent the pace of real work.

A same-day response can include a constraint. "We design and build with one small team, and a store migration needs a staging pass before any DNS change." That sentence helps the sender more than a mood board. It is still a reply, not a delivery.

It can include a decline. Same-day includes the courtesy of a prompt no when the project wants a discipline the studio does not practice, or a timeline that would require cutting the review that makes the work careful. A fast no is a complete response.

[Nielsen Norman Group's research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is a reminder about the length of the reply itself. Jakob Nielsen wrote in 2011 that people often leave a web page in 10 to 20 seconds, and that they have time to read only about a quarter of the text on pages they visit. Email is a different surface, and the hurry is familiar. Put the next step in the first lines. The reasoning can follow for the person who wants it.

## How to read a reply that says "not yet"

"Not yet" is a responsible same-day answer when the question asks for a commitment. A launch date before the scope exists, a fixed price before the pages are listed, a promise that search rankings will survive a replatform: these should come back as the condition under which an answer becomes possible.

The condition should be specific. "Send the current URL, the name of the approver, and whether the offer has changed since the site was written. Then we can say whether this is a revamp or a rebuild." The sender leaves with a task, not a mood.

A reply that says "excited to learn more" and stops is a delayed no, or a delayed yes, wearing a friendly sentence. Ask for the next step if it is missing. A studio that cannot name one on the same day is telling you something about the communication you would live with later.

## Email, the call, and the project thread

These are three different rooms.

Email is the front door. A same-day human answer lives here, including for people who are not yet clients. Use it when you want a person to read a short description of the work and tell you the next step.

The intro call is the second room. It should decide fit, a rough shape of the work, and whether a proposal is worth writing. It is a scheduled conversation, not a faster email. Bringing a rough offer and the current URL makes the half hour decisive.

The project thread is the third room, and it starts only after the work is agreed. There, same-day means something narrower: a decision or a blocker is acknowledged the day it is raised, with the effect on the date. It still does not mean a new screen by evening. The build has a cadence. The cadence is the speed of craft. The same-day note is the speed of honesty.

Mixing the rooms upsets both. Treating production like the front door produces shallow work delivered in a rush. Treating the front door like production means a founder waits days to learn whether anyone read the email.

## What you can send so the reply is easy

A short note gets a better answer. Say who the site or product is for, what the one action should be, the current URL if it exists, and the timing you are actually facing. Three sentences are enough. An attachment of a forty-page deck asks the reader to do unpaid synthesis before they can answer.

Say if you are writing to several studios. A same-day reply can still be thoughtful when the sender is comparing options. Pretending otherwise wastes the first exchange.

If you already know you want the second room, you can book an [intro call with Hanabi](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) directly. The email remains the right door when you want a human answer before you put time on a calendar.

Once a project is underway, the same-day habit has to sit inside a larger cadence or it becomes a stream of pings. [Communication habits that keep a build on track](/blog/communication-that-keeps-a-build-on-track) is the next piece, because a fast reply still needs a shared channel and a written decision to keep the build honest.
